goal_title: Book: Arrays and Regularity — improvements from the spine reading
why: The whole spine was read as a book on 2026-09-24, one sequence at a time, and every stumble, false claim or broken handover in array_tutorial became a task Palle can pick up one at a time. Reader: the VR visitor.
success_criteria: every open task here is done or skipped with a note
the chapters read through without a stumble in the headset
every code excerpt and number in the chapters matches the source

book.title: Arrays and Regularity
chapters_read: Trans_Pit (last of transformation, for the handover in)
Color_Context_Placed (first of color, for the handover out)

reading.arc: The sequence takes the pickup cube from Transformation and multiplies it. Array gives the copies numbers: a row and a two-index grid whose tables record absence when a cube is collected by contact, then Molnár's nested cubes show that each address can host its own bounded departure. Tutorial_3D adds the third index and, separately, the permission to reach it: the visitor flies inside a glass enclosure, collects a cube, and watches the console write a zero while the address stays. The address then receives a motif: one black-and-white diagonal tile placed under six rules underfoot (Floor), the same six stood up as walls, ending at a hinged section of the museum's own enclosure that turns open onto a landing outside (Walls). Finally the grid gets clocks: a disco floor whose values change while its tiles stay put, and a step sequencer whose playhead reads a boolean score, the two clocks shown to be separate and only loosely coupled by a flash (Disco). The through-line is slot versus value versus the act of reading, and the body that meets all three.
holds: The carried cube: 'This is the cube we met at the beginning of Transformation' opens Array; the same pickup cube fills the row, the grid and the 4x4x4 volume, and collection by contact is what writes a zero in every table.

The remainder refrain, cross-referenced on purpose: range(4) ends at three (Array), 'after three it returns to zero' at the flight console (3D), '%4' quarter turns 'You met that return at the flight console' (Floor), '(x+z+phase)%2' and 'step % 12' (Disco).

Address / value / reading / passage held apart in every hall: 'The number naming the slot and the number stored there do different jobs' (Array); 'The third index has extended what we can address. Flight has extended what we can reach' (3D); 'The first changed what we could read; the second changed where we could go' (Walls); 'Distinguish the score, the floor's independent animation and your movement' (Disco).
The exception as a recurring device: ONE EXCEPTION on the floor, on the wall, shared by the hinged sheet, then 'Put a beat somewhere that interrupts the repetition you expected' (Disco).

One-question openers and a closing hand-off sentence in every chapter that names the next hall's move ('First, let the same six rules stand up'; 'The next floor will add a clock'; 'Next, our familiar forms gather in coloured stacks').
Black and white as a declared constraint before Color: 'We have limited the palette to make the arrangement easier to compare' (Floor), 'Here the floor is black and white again' (Disco).

hall_notes.note: The overture: the row and its table, the plate-addressed grid and its table, a comparison of the two empty places, then Molnár's nested cubes with three sliders and a depth button; closes by promising a hall above the head. The longest chapter by a factor of two and it earns most of it, but four of the hall's seven works (a second line of four cubes, an xyz gadget, a wandering grid agent with a caption, a pulsar visualizer by the exit) are never mentioned.

One artifact: the console that steps X/Y/Z, flight inside the glass box, collection by contact, storage order y,z,x versus display order x,y,z, then hovering in a recorded absence. Tight and well judged, except that its flight paragraph is a manual with desktop keys, and it sends the reader out to the console and back in for a check that could be done in one pass.

Six fields from one tile, TURN MOTIF and EXCEPTION at the entrance console, the (cx+cy)%4 line tied back to the flight console, then the flat-image versus collision distinction ('Your eye can find a ridge where your foot finds no step'). The rule list is brisk but each rule gets a verb, and every claim matches the generator.

The same six fields upright, distance and perspective doing work, then the hinged section of the enclosure and the landing outside: the sequence's high point, where the museum's thin skin is looked at from behind. All mechanics (waits while occupied, pauses mid-turn, plain reverse) match the code; one orientation cue points the wrong way and the sheet stretches the image without the text saying so.

Floor console (hold, single step, pattern, speed), the SUPER TRIANGLE families, the sequencer's grid, then the two clocks pulled apart and the step%12 flash that cannot tell 0 from 12. Well staged and true to the bridge code; a couple of spatial cues ('Beside it') and one code-formatted paraphrase would trip a reader who looks for what they name.

stumbles: Array: 'Find the four numbered positions' - the hall holds two lines of four plated cubes (row_3_x at (3,6), column_3_z at (15,5)); the column, the xyz gadget, the grid agent and the pulsar are never mentioned.

Array: a cyan sphere with a running caption ('Searching...', 'Consuming (XP: n)') wanders the hall, removing or copying a structure cube every couple of seconds, in a chapter asking 'what can happen at an address' that never names it.
Array (Molnár): 'Select one layer and reset the changes' names neither button (they read DEPTH n / 4 and RESET), and the reader is not told the study arrives already disturbed.

Tutorial_3D: 'On desktop, look and use WASD, with Space to rise and Ctrl to descend. In VR, the left stick follows the tilted left controller.' - desktop keys in reader prose, and the VR sentence does not tell a headset visitor what to do with the controller.

Tutorial_3D: 'Return to the console and select that address' comes before 'Hover where a cube used to be' - the console stands outside the enclosure, so the reader is sent out through a door and back in.
Tutorial_Tiling_Walls: 'Near the far end, on the right' - the hinged section is in the east boundary; the spawn faces the hall's works (+Z), so east is on the visitor's left, past ONE EXCEPTION.

Tutorial_Tiling_Walls: 'the same pattern reaches a narrow part of the museum wall' - the square image is stretched onto a 1.94 x 4.44 m face, so the triangles are about 2.3 times taller than on the panels; a visitor comparing sees a different shape.
Tutorial_Disco: 'Beside it, the sequencer has another' - the sequencer is six cells from the console, across the entrance.
Tutorial_Disco: 'The remainder returns here as `step % 12`' is set as code but the source reads step % disco_floor.grid_width; the 12 is a map token.
Figures: three of the six (two-turns, fixed-addresses-changing-values, triangle-combinations) carry the desktop hand-inventory HUD 'mushrooms ..... [F]' in the corner.

keep.quote: The number naming the slot and the number stored there do different jobs.
An empty slot can still have an address.
We have repeated the cube, but we do not have to repeat its fate. At each address, another decision becomes possible.
You can pass between two named places without arriving at another. The array gives us a way to address its cubes; it does not number every position your body can occupy.
The third index has extended what we can address. Flight has extended what we can reach. Keep those changes separate as you descend.
Your eye can find a ridge where your foot finds no step.
Room after room, a thin enclosure kept an inside around our forward walk. Here we can look at its other side.
Sharing a space with a rhythm is different from being measured by it.

reading.handover_in: Trans_Pit closes on the airlock built from the three operations and asks 'What else could these three operations make possible?'. Array opens 'This is the cube we met at the beginning of Transformation... Here it has company' and answers the question in its Molnár region ('These are the operations we brought from Transformation, now applied throughout an array'). The object (the pickup cube, collected by walking into it since Trans_Pre) and the question both carry. The only seam is that the door-as-welcome image is dropped without a glance back; acceptable, not a task.
reading.handover_out: Tutorial_Disco closes 'Next, our familiar forms gather in coloured stacks. A stored value can assign a colour to a surface. What happens when that colour meets its neighbours?'. Color_Context_Placed opens by naming arrays ('each with an address in a list') and the disco floor by name ('the positions stayed fixed while the pattern changed'), and its fourth column delivers 'A neighbour has become an input'. Clean; the promise and the pickup match exactly.
reading_errors: 'a captioned cyan sphere' (Array stumble, also task index 1): the agent's colour is set from its tier - `gridagent:copy` -> TIER_1_COPY -> Color(0.5,0.8,1.0), light blue (evolution_tiers.gd:86; set_tier at grid_agent_base.gd:635-640 overrides the CYAN default at :63, called from GridInteractablesComponent.gd:1043).

'two lines of four plated cubes (row_3_x at (3,6), column_3_z at (15,5))' (Array stumble, also task index 3): the row is not plated - row_3_x.gd:58-66 hangs a billboard '[i]' label on each cube, which is what the chapter's 'the cube took its label with it' describes; only column_3_z carries `#notation:plate`.

'The longest chapter by a factor of two' (Array hall note): 1198 words against Disco's 879 is 1.36x; it is twice only the two shortest chapters (585 each). The five word counts themselves match wc -w exactly.

'a pulsar visualizer by the exit' (Array hall note): pulsar_visualizer stands at (3,19), seven cells west of the exit teleporter (10,21) and the far door (9-11,22) - near the far wall, not by the exit. Minor.
'three sliders and a depth button' (Array hall note): the study has two buttons, DEPTH and RESET (molnar_cube_study.gd:158-166). Minor omission.

NOTE (not an error): the summary text was truncated mid-'stumbles' after the Tutorial_Tiling_Walls entry, so anything past it was not reviewed. Everything else checked out: seven works with four unmentioned; button names PATTERN, PLAY / HOLD, ONE STEP, SPEED (disco_controls.gd:28-33) and DEPTH n / 4, RESET; the turning-wall mechanics (wall_exception.gd:40, :97-116); storage order values[y][z][x] (array_flight_lab.gd:22-25); the flash-while-held coupling (StandaloneDiscoFloor.gd:29,:69 auto_start keeps is_running true; HOLD only stops the console's clock).

dropped.title: Trim the third Molnár disclaimer
dropped.reason: Lines confirmed (Array/final.md:51, :59, :69), but this is taste, not a defect a headset visitor meets. The three mentions serve three reading modes - the prose ('takes its starting point from'), the caption ('spatial interpretation after Molnár', a genre label) and the citation - and the footnote's second sentence is the only one that says what is NOT claimed ('her drawing or algorithm'), the same scope statement the artifact itself carries (molnar_cube_study.gd:2, registry description). A footnote is where that belongs; deleting it removes information to save eighteen words.

Code confirmed: museum_flight_provider.gd:22-26 builds the VR velocity from the left controller's global_basis and its "primary" stick and passes no vertical term (flight_velocity's `vertical` defaults to 0.0); museum_flight_box.gd:31-33 `direction = view.x*axes.x - view.z*axes.y`, :30 "Neutral input hovers"; WASD/Space/Ctrl exist only in desktop_velocity :35-39; the sign at :105 already carries both lines, so a desktop walker loses nothing. One mapping in the proposal is wrong: with the stick forward you travel along the controller's own forward (-view.z), so pitching it up climbs and down descends, but "tilt it sideways to drift" is not what the code does - rolling the controller leaves its -Z unchanged; sideways travel comes from pushing the stick sideways (view.x*axes.x, the controller's right).

tasks.title: Name the grid agent that edits the floor
tasks.spec:
[prose] Array
Quote: “An array needs a way to distinguish its entries; it does not require them to look alike, stand straight or remain occupied.”
Why: The visitor meets a captioned light-blue sphere that removes or copies a structure cube every couple of seconds while the chapter is silent; the sequence notes call it 'the only object in the ladder that writes into an array without you', which is exactly this chapter's question. The museum embeds the real grid for this hall and its disarm pass does not stop the agent, so Palle should first check in the headset whether it opens holes in the deck; if it does, fix the map or the disarm pass before writing it in.
Do: After that sentence, once the headset check is clean, add: 'Something else is writing here. The small sphere wandering the floor reads the room's own grid the way the tables read theirs, and every few seconds it takes a cube or copies one, without asking. Watch a cell it has visited. Which record would have to change for the tables to know?'

tasks.title: Collect, hover, then descend to the console
tasks.spec:
[structure] Tutorial_3D
Quote: “Choose an address, approach its cube and collect it by contact. Return to the console and select that address. Its value is now zero.”
Why: The console stands outside the glass box and flight stops at its faces, so this order sends the visitor out through a door, then back in for 'Hover where a cube used to be' two paragraphs later. One pass reads better and matches the figure, which shows the hover and the zero together.
Do: Reorder into one pass: 'At the console, select an address and read it. Walk through the doorway, rise to the marker and collect its cube by contact.'
